summary: This Britannica article excerpt explains that colour is a property of light, which is electromagnetic radiation whose visible range spans roughly 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). It gives a table of spectral colours with wavelength, frequency and energy values, then covers the laws of colour mixture: additive mixing of light (with red, green and blue as primaries and Newton's colour circle) and subtractive mixing of pigments and filters (with cyan, magenta and yellow as primaries). It closes by explaining why common naming confusions arise between subtractive and additive primaries.
one_line: Britannica article section explaining the visible spectrum of light and the additive and subtractive laws of colour mixture.
key_facts: Newton demonstrated that colour is a quality of light.
Light is a form of electromagnetic radiation with properties of both waves and particles.
Wavelengths of visible light range from about 400 nm at the violet end to 700 nm at the red end of the spectrum.
The limits of the visible spectrum are not sharply defined and vary among individuals.
The name photon is used for the smallest quantity of light of any given wavelength.
The energy of a photon is directly proportional to frequency and inversely proportional to wavelength.
The eye can distinguish some 10 million colours, all deriving from additive and subtractive light mixture.
Newton's colour circle combines the spectral colours red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, indigo and blue-violet with the nonspectral colour magenta.
The three additive primary colours are red, green, and blue.
White is produced at the centre of Newton's colour circle by mixing complementary colours such as yellow and blue-violet.
Subtractive colour mixing occurs when colorants such as pigments or dyes are mixed or when coloured filters are inserted into a beam of white light.
If a projector is fitted with both red and green filters, all colours are absorbed and no light is transmitted, resulting in black.
A yellow pigment absorbs blue and violet light while reflecting yellow, green, and red light.
The subtractive primaries are cyan, magenta, and yellow.
The subtractive primary cyan is properly a blue-green, and the subtractive primary magenta is commonly called red, which causes confusion.

entities.name: Isaac Newton

entities.name: Newton's colour circle
entities.role: Colour circle first devised by Newton, still widely used for colour design, combining spectral and nonspectral colours.

entities.name: RGB colour model
entities.role: One of the three main colour models, an additive model used in digital devices and light-based media.

entities.name: Photon
entities.role: Name for the smallest quantity of light of any given wavelength, encompassing light's wave and particle duality.
